WITH ci AS (                                   -- the first tap starts the wait
  SELECT order_id, MIN(event_ts) AS checkin_ts
  FROM pickup_events WHERE event_type = 'checkin'
  GROUP BY order_id
), ho AS (
  SELECT order_id, MIN(event_ts) AS handover_ts
  FROM pickup_events WHERE event_type = 'handover'
  GROUP BY order_id
), w AS (
  SELECT o.store_id, s.tz,
         GREATEST(ci.checkin_ts, o.slot_start) AS wait_start,
         ho.handover_ts
  FROM pickup_orders o
  JOIN stores s ON s.store_id = o.store_id
  JOIN ci ON ci.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN ho ON ho.order_id = o.order_id
), m AS (
  SELECT store_id,
         EXTRACT(HOUR FROM wait_start AT TIME ZONE tz)::int              AS hour_of_day,
         GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM handover_ts - wait_start) / 60, 0)  AS wait_min
  FROM w
)
SELECT store_id, hour_of_day,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS handovers,
       ROUND(AVG(wait_min), 1)                         AS avg_wait_min,
       MAX(wait_min)                                   AS max_wait_min,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE wait_min > {{target}})   AS over_target
FROM m
GROUP BY store_id, hour_of_day
ORDER BY store_id, hour_of_day;

Explanation. Reduce the events to one row per order (first check-in, the handover); the inner joins drop orders missing either. The wait clock starts at GREATEST(checkin, slot_start), so an early customer is measured from the slot start, and the clamp at 0 covers a handover made before the slot started. The hour is taken from the wait start, not the check-in, converted to the store's zone with AT TIME ZONE tz (a timestamptz at a zone name gives the local wall-clock time). Because times are whole minutes, every wait is an exact number of minutes and ROUND(AVG(…), 1) has no floating-point surprises.

Complexity. Two hash aggregates over the events, a hash join with orders and stores, and a final aggregate: O(n) apart from the small sort for the output. In production this is an incremental daily job keyed by order.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_DIFF(handover_ts, wait_start, SECOND) / 60, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM DATETIME(wait_start, tz)), COUNTIF. Snowflake: DATEDIFF('second', …) / 60, HOUR(CONVERT_TIMEZONE(tz, wait_start)), COUNT_IF; GREATEST returns NULL if either argument is NULL in all three engines. Spark SQL: unix_timestamp differences, hour(from_utc_timestamp(wait_start, tz)). MySQL 8: TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …) and CONVERT_TZ (needs the time zone tables loaded).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: an early check-in in the previous clock hour whose wait is exactly the target; a check-in at minute 59 of an hour. Hard: a second "I'm here" tap during the wait; an order checked in but never handed over; a handover with no check-in; a handover before the slot started (wait 0, otherwise negative); a check-in exactly at the slot start. Very Hard: stores in several US time zones and a slot at 8 pm local that falls on the next UTC day.

Common mistakes. Measuring from the check-in for early customers; grouping by the check-in hour; using the last check-in; a negative wait for an early handover; >= for "over the target"; extracting the hour in UTC; inner-joining the events in a way that multiplies rows when an order has two check-ins (the average and count both inflate); averaging per-hour averages.

Follow-up guidance. (1) percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY wait_min); percentiles are not additive, so a regional p90 needs the raw waits or a mergeable sketch (t-digest, KLL). (2) Report the share of handovers with no check-in beside the wait metric, per store and hour; a store with many walk-ups has a less representative wait. (3) Compare like with like: the same hours before and after, with order counts shown, or a weighted average using a fixed hour mix. (4) Partition events by event date; keep an open-orders state keyed by order id, finalise an order when its handover arrives, and allow late handovers to update the hour bucket they belong to (the bucket is fixed by the wait start, which is known at check-in).

WITH latest AS (                              -- the latest offer per line decides
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id, line_no) order_id, line_no, decision
  FROM sub_offers
  ORDER BY order_id, line_no, offered_ts DESC, offer_id DESC
), l AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('week', o.pickup_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS week_start,
         i.category,
         ol.pick_status = 'short' AND lt.order_id IS NOT NULL                              AS substituted,
         ol.pick_status = 'short' AND lt.order_id IS NOT NULL AND lt.decision = 'rejected' AS rejected,
         ol.pick_status = 'short' AND lt.order_id IS NULL AND ol.allow_sub                 AS missed
  FROM order_lines ol
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = ol.order_id
  JOIN items i ON i.item_id = ol.item_id
  LEFT JOIN latest lt ON lt.order_id = ol.order_id AND lt.line_no = ol.line_no
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT week_start, category,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS lines,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE substituted)        AS substituted,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rejected)           AS rejected,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rejected)::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE substituted), 0), 4) AS reject_rate,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE missed)             AS short_no_offer
FROM l
GROUP BY week_start, category
ORDER BY week_start, category;

Explanation. One latest offer per line (DISTINCT ON with offered_ts DESC, offer_id DESC), left-joined to the lines of completed orders, so each line is classified once: substituted (short with an offer), rejected (its latest decision is rejected; a NULL decision is not), missed (short, no offer, substitutes allowed). An offer on a picked line exists in the data but cannot make the line substituted. The category comes from the ordered item. date_trunc('week', …) on the UTC timestamp returns the Monday, and NULLIF turns an empty denominator into a NULL rate.

Complexity. One sort of the offers for DISTINCT ON, hash joins and one hash aggregate: O(n log n) in the offers, O(n) in the lines.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, line_no ORDER BY offered_ts DESC, offer_id DESC) = 1, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(pickup_ts), ISOWEEK), COUNTIF, SAFE_DIVIDE. Snowflake: QUALIFY, DATE_TRUNC('week', …) whose first day depends on WEEK_START (default Monday under the ISO-like default, but check the session), COUNT_IF, DIV0NULL-style handling. Spark SQL: date_trunc('week', …) starts on Monday; max_by(decision, struct(offered_ts, offer_id)) picks the latest decision. MySQL 8: ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE and SUM(CASE …); weeks via DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL WEEKDAY(d) DAY).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: a rejected substitution on Sunday night and an accepted one on Monday morning (UTC) for the same item, one substitute from another category, and a short line with no offer. Hard: a line rejected then accepted on a second offer; a NULL decision (accepted by this exercise's rule); a cancelled order with a rejection and a missed offer. Very Hard: an offer on a line that was then picked; a short line with allow_sub = false.

Common mistakes. Dividing by all short lines; grouping by the substitute's category; Sunday-start weeks; the first offer instead of the latest; counting NULL as rejected or dropping it from the denominator; including cancelled orders; an inner join that loses missed offers; counting offers rather than lines (a line with two offers counted twice); a rate of 0 instead of NULL.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Grain becomes (week, ordered category, substitute item); the denominator is lines whose latest offer used that substitute; small counts need a minimum before ranking. (2) Local dates move evening pickups in western stores to the previous UTC day only rarely here, but at scale near midnight the weekly totals shift slightly; for a trend the rule matters less than keeping it fixed. (3) Rejected substitutions lose the ordered item's revenue (refund); missed offers lose it too; use the order-time price, not today's. (4) Partition by pickup date; recompute only weeks that received offers or decisions since the last run (a watermark on offered_ts and order updates), and close a week after the latest possible handover.

WITH store_list AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT store_id FROM sales
), days AS (                                   -- each store's open days, newest first
  SELECT s.store_id, d::date AS biz_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY s.store_id ORDER BY d DESC) AS rn
  FROM store_list s
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(DATE '{{first_day}}', DATE '{{as_of}}', interval '1 day') AS d
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM store_closures c
                    WHERE c.store_id = s.store_id AND c.biz_date = d::date)
), store_items AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT store_id, item_id FROM sales
), daily AS (                                  -- net units per store, item and day
  SELECT store_id, item_id, biz_date, SUM(units) AS net
  FROM sales
  GROUP BY store_id, item_id, biz_date
), grid AS (
  SELECT si.store_id, si.item_id, d.rn,
         COALESCE(dl.net, 0) AS net,
         sn.on_hand
  FROM store_items si
  JOIN days d ON d.store_id = si.store_id AND d.rn <= 3 + {{baseline_days}}
  LEFT JOIN daily dl ON dl.store_id = si.store_id AND dl.item_id = si.item_id AND dl.biz_date = d.biz_date
  LEFT JOIN inventory_snapshots sn ON sn.store_id = si.store_id AND sn.item_id = si.item_id AND sn.biz_date = d.biz_date
)
SELECT store_id, item_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rn > 3 AND net > 0) AS baseline_days_sold,
       SUM(net) FILTER (WHERE rn > 3)            AS baseline_units,
       MAX(on_hand) FILTER (WHERE rn = 1)        AS on_hand
FROM grid
GROUP BY store_id, item_id
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rn <= 3 AND on_hand > 0) = 3
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rn <= 3 AND net > 0) = 0
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rn > 3 AND net > 0) >= {{min_days}}
ORDER BY store_id, item_id;

Explanation. A spine of each store's open days, numbered back from the as-of date, turns both windows into ranges of rn: 1–3 is the check window, 4 to 3 + baseline the baseline. Sales are netted per day first and joined onto the spine, so a day with no row is 0 and a day with only a return is not a sale. A missing snapshot gives NULL, which fails on_hand > 0, so the store-item needs three positive snapshots. Everything else is conditional counting in one aggregate.

Complexity. The spine is stores × days; the grid is store-items × (3 + baseline) days; one aggregate over sales and one over the grid. Linear in the rows read. Daily in production, this reads only the last few weeks of a date-partitioned sales table.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(first, as_of)) for the spine, COUNTIF, QUALIFY not needed. Snowflake: a spine from TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n)) with DATEADD, COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: explode(sequence(first, as_of, interval 1 day)), count_if. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE for the spine, SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: a suspect that sold on exactly the threshold of baseline days; an item that sold on one day too few in the baseline but also on the day just before the baseline (a window one day too long makes it a suspect); a store-item that sold out (0 on hand) during the check window; items that sold in the check window. Hard: a check day with only a return, a check day with a zero row, a missing snapshot on a check day. Very Hard: several rows per day to net (including a sale and a matching return), store closures inside the check window and the baseline.

Common mistakes. A baseline of baseline + 1 days, or one that overlaps the check window; > instead of >= for the threshold; counting a day as sold whenever a row exists; ignoring missing snapshots (COALESCE(on_hand, 1) or an inner join that silently drops the day and then checks only the days present); calendar windows when the store was closed; window frames over rows (ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING) on a sales table that has no row for quiet days.

Follow-up guidance. (1) With a daily rate λ from the baseline, the chance of three quiet days by luck is about e^(−3λ) under a Poisson assumption; flag when that falls below a chosen level. State it as a model, not a fact. (2) A delivery during the window that still did not sell is stronger evidence (more stock and no sales), unless the delivery is not yet on the shelf. (3) Precision: the share of checked suspects whose count was corrected downwards; track it per category, and cap the list per store so teams can act. (4) Keep a rolling per-store-item state (last sale date, baseline counts) updated daily from one day of sales, rather than rescanning a month.

Rubric anchors. 2: right idea but windows off by one, returns counted as sales, or missing snapshots treated as stock. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also proposes a rate-based rule, measures precision and computes incrementally.

Strong signals. Builds a date spine before anything else; asks about closures, returns and missing snapshots. Red flags. Calling the suspects shrink or theft; blaming store associates for counts.

def range_sales(n_minutes, ops):
    n = n_minutes
    tree = [0] * (n + 1)                # Fenwick tree over minutes, 1-based

    def add(i, v):
        i += 1
        while i <= n:
            tree[i] += v
            i += i & -i

    def prefix(i):                      # total of minutes 0 .. i-1
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += tree[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s

    txns = {}                           # txn_id -> [minute, cents, counted]
    void_first = set()                  # voids that arrived before their sale
    out = []
    for op in ops:
        kind = op[0]
        if kind == 'query':
            lo, hi = op[1], op[2]
            out.append(prefix(hi + 1) - prefix(lo) if lo <= hi else 0)
        elif kind == 'sale':
            _, tid, minute, cents = op
            counted = tid not in void_first
            txns[tid] = [minute, cents, counted]
            if counted:
                add(minute, cents)
        elif kind == 'void':
            t = txns.get(op[1])
            if t is None:
                void_first.add(op[1])
            elif t[2]:
                t[2] = False
                add(t[0], -t[1])
        else:                           # move
            t = txns.get(op[1])
            if t is not None:
                if t[2]:
                    add(t[0], -t[1])
                    add(op[2], t[1])
                t[0] = op[2]
    return out

Explanation. Two pieces of state. A dict holds each transaction's current minute, amount and whether it still counts; it makes voids and moves O(1) to locate and makes repeated voids harmless. A Fenwick tree over minutes holds the counted total per minute and answers prefix totals in O(log n); a range is the difference of two prefixes. A sale adds its amount, a void subtracts it at the transaction's current minute, and a move subtracts at the old minute and adds at the new one, all only while the transaction counts. A void for a transaction not seen yet is remembered, so the sale arrives already voided; a move for an unknown transaction is ignored as specified.

Complexity. O(log n) per sale, void, move and query; O(n) memory for the tree plus O(T) for the transactions. The timing test (525 600 minutes, 120 000 sales with about 12 000 voids and 12 000 moves, 30 000 queries averaging a third of the year) ran in about 0.6–0.75 s in CPython at every level. Re-summing each range with sum(per_minute[lo:hi + 1]) (C-speed summing) took about 90 s on the same input; rebuilding prefix sums with itertools.accumulate whenever an update came before a query (the likely "middle" approach) did not finish within 120 s, because almost every query follows an update. A square-root decomposition (blocks of about 725 minutes with block totals) is O(√n) per query and passes; accept it as a correct, slower alternative and ask for its costs.

Dialect notes. Java/C++: a long[] Fenwick tree and a HashMap; totals of a year of sales in cents need 64-bit integers. In a warehouse the same question is answered with a per-minute table and window sums or a pre-aggregated cube, recomputed when late data lands; the in-memory structure is for interactive answers over data that is still changing. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A late sale into a minute inside a range already answered; both ends of a range included and a one-minute range; a void inside a range. Hard: a move between minutes; a repeated void; a voided transaction that is moved; lo > hi returning 0; the first and last minutes. Very Hard: a void that arrives before its sale (and is repeated after it), a move for a transaction not seen yet, and a transaction voided before arrival and then moved.

Common mistakes. Off-by-one in the 1-based tree (prefix(hi) instead of prefix(hi + 1)); subtracting a void at the original minute after a move; subtracting twice on a repeated void; moving a voided transaction's amount back into the totals; treating lo > hi as an error or as a swapped range; rebuilding prefix sums on every query.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A range maximum of 15-minute sums is a segment tree over 15-minute window sums; each point update changes up to 15 windows, so an update is O(15 log n) with a range-add segment tree with lazy propagation, or precompute window sums and use a segment tree storing max with range add. (2) Per store and department, keep one tree per key (memory grows with keys × minutes); a 2-D Fenwick tree suits a fixed small grid of dimensions; at larger cardinality pre-aggregate into hour blocks and correct within the edges. (3) Cheap updates and slower queries: buffer updates and apply in batches before each query, or use blocks; queries few per second can afford O(√n). (4) Load corrections as append-only adjustment rows, recompute affected minute and hour aggregates by partition, and keep the adjustment history for audit; you lose instant answers between loads.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct with per-minute totals and a sum per query, or a Fenwick tree with void/move bookkeeping errors. 3: all tests pass with log-time updates and queries. 4: also explains the alternatives (segment tree, blocks), the follow-up structures and warehouse trade-offs.

Strong signals. Separates transaction state from the minute structure; asks what a void of an unknown or voided transaction means. Red flags. Rebuilding everything on every operation; ignoring that moves and voids interact.

from collections import deque


def expired_units(lots, sales, writeoffs, as_of):
    left = {lot_id: units for lot_id, _, _, units, _ in lots}
    expiry = {lot_id: exp for lot_id, _, _, _, exp in lots}
    shelf = {}                                   # item -> deque of lot ids, oldest first
    li = wi = 0
    for day, item, units in sales:
        while li < len(lots) and lots[li][2] <= day:            # deliveries up to today
            lot_id, it = lots[li][0], lots[li][1]
            shelf.setdefault(it, deque()).append(lot_id)
            li += 1
        while wi < len(writeoffs) and writeoffs[wi][0] <= day:  # write-offs up to today
            wday, lot_id, n = writeoffs[wi]
            if wday <= expiry[lot_id]:
                left[lot_id] -= min(n, left[lot_id])
            wi += 1
        q = shelf.get(item)
        while units and q:
            lot_id = q[0]
            if left[lot_id] == 0 or expiry[lot_id] < day:       # sold out or past its date
                q.popleft()
                continue
            take = min(units, left[lot_id])
            left[lot_id] -= take
            units -= take
    for wday, lot_id, n in writeoffs[wi:]:                      # write-offs after the last sale
        if wday <= expiry[lot_id]:
            left[lot_id] -= min(n, left[lot_id])
    return {lot_id: left[lot_id] for lot_id, *_ in lots if expiry[lot_id] < as_of}

Explanation. A deque of lot ids per item, in delivery order, is exactly the oldest-first order. A sale looks at the front: a lot that is sold out, or whose expiry day is before today, can never sell again (days only move forward), so it leaves the queue for good; otherwise the sale takes what it can and continues. A lot that expires while a still-sellable older lot is in front of it simply waits in the queue and is discarded when it reaches the front. Write-offs touch a named lot's count directly, before the sales of their day, and are ignored after the expiry day. After its expiry day nothing changes a lot's count, so the units left are its expired units.

Complexity. Each lot enters and leaves its queue once, and each step of a sale either removes a lot or finishes the sale: O(n + L + W) for n sales, L lots and W write-offs, amortised. The timing test (5 items, 50 000 lots, 125 000 sales over 3 000 days) ran in about 0.3 s in CPython. Scanning an item's lots from the oldest on every sale took about 80 s by extrapolation (1.8 s at 15% of the size, quadratic growth). The likely "middle" approach, a per-item pointer that skips sold-out lots but keeps re-scanning expired ones, did not finish within 200 s, because expired lots pile up in front of the pointer. A per-item list with pop(0) for removals is O(L) per removal in theory but passes here (the memmove is fast at these sizes); accept it and ask for its cost.

Dialect notes. Java: ArrayDeque<Integer> per item in a HashMap. C++: std::deque. In SQL, FIFO allocation of sales to lots is done with running totals: cumulative supply per item by delivery order against cumulative demand, joined on overlapping ranges; expiry makes it iterative, so a procedural pass (or a recursive CTE) is usually clearer. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A sale on the expiry day; a lot sold on its delivery day; the as_of boundary (expiry on as_of is left out, one day earlier included); a sale that spans two lots. def expired_units(lots, sales, writeoffs, as_of):
    left = {lot_id: units for lot_id, _, _, units, _ in lots}
    expiry = {lot_id: exp for lot_id, _, _, _, exp in lots}
    shelf = {}                                   # item -> deque of lot ids, oldest first
    li = wi = 0
    for day, item, units in sales:
        while li < len(lots) and lots[li][2] <= day:            # deliveries up to today
            lot_id, it = lots[li][0], lots[li][1]
            shelf.setdefault(it, deque()).append(lot_id)
            li += 1
        while wi < len(writeoffs) and writeoffs[wi][0] <= day:  # write-offs up to today
            wday, lot_id, n = writeoffs[wi]
            if wday <= expiry[lot_id]:
                left[lot_id] -= min(n, left[lot_id])
            wi += 1
        q = shelf.get(item)
        while units and q:
            lot_id = q[0]
            if left[lot_id] == 0 or expiry[lot_id] < day:       # sold out or past its date
                q.popleft()
                continue
            take = min(units, left[lot_id])
            left[lot_id] -= take
            units -= take
    for wday, lot_id, n in writeoffs[wi:]:                      # write-offs after the last sale
        if wday <= expiry[lot_id]:
            left[lot_id] -= min(n, left[lot_id])
    return {lot_id: left[lot_id] for lot_id, *_ in lots if expiry[lot_id] < as_of}

from itertools import combinations


def frequent_pairs(baskets, s, max_items=None):
    counts = {}
    for basket in baskets:
        items = sorted(set(basket))                 # repeats removed, name order
        if max_items is not None and len(items) > max_items:
            continue                                 # a bulk basket: no pair is generated
        for pair in combinations(items, 2):
            counts[pair] = counts.get(pair, 0) + 1
    out = [(a, b, c) for (a, b), c in counts.items() if c >= s]
    out.sort(key=lambda t: (-t[2], t[0], t[1]))
    return out

Explanation. The pairs that can ever reach the threshold are the pairs that occur inside some basket, so count exactly those. Each basket is reduced to its sorted set of distinct items. That removes repeated scans, makes sure an item never pairs with itself, and makes combinations emit every pair already in name order a < b. A dictionary keyed by the pair counts baskets. The threshold is inclusive. The final sort uses (-count, a, b). Under the bulk rule, the distinct-item count is checked before any pair is produced: a basket of 4 000 items holds about eight million pairs, so a filter applied after counting is far too late.

Complexity. O(Σ b²) pair increments, where b is the number of distinct items in each counted basket, plus O(Σ |basket| log b) to deduplicate and sort, plus O(P log P) to sort the P qualifying pairs. Memory is O(distinct pairs seen). The timing tests (40 000 to 50 000 baskets over 4 000 to 5 000 items, about 650 000 pairs; Very Hard adds 30 bulk baskets of 4 000 items) run in about 0.3 to 0.4 s in CPython. The likely "middle" approach is Apriori-style: keep a set of basket ids per item, prune items with support below s, then intersect the sets for every pair of remaining items. At these sizes almost every item survives the pruning (each appears in about 45 baskets, against s of 15 or 20), so it is 8 to 12 million intersections. It takes 11 to 18 s, over the 8 s limit and 30 to 45 times slower than counting in baskets. Scanning every basket for every pair of catalogue items is O(I²·n), about 10¹² checks. Counting pairs before applying max_items spends about 240 million increments on the bulk baskets alone.

Dialect notes. In SQL this is a self-join of distinct basket lines on the basket id with a.item < b.item, then GROUP BY a.item, b.item HAVING COUNT(*) >= s. Deduplicate lines first (SELECT DISTINCT basket_id, item), and filter bulk baskets with a HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT item) <= max_items subquery before the join, or the join explodes in the same way. In Spark, flatMap each basket to its pairs and reduceByKey; skew comes from very popular items, not from the pair count. In Java or C++, pack two item indices into one 64-bit key rather than allocating a pair object for each increment. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A pair in exactly s baskets (included) and in s − 1 (excluded); items scanned in reverse name order; ties in count ordered by a then b; s = 1; an item listed twice (counted once, never paired with itself); empty and one-item baskets; no qualifying pair (empty list); at Very Hard, a basket with exactly max_items distinct items (counted), one more (skipped), and repeats that do not push a basket over the limit.

Common mistakes. Counting a pair twice when an item is listed twice; pairing an item with itself; emitting (b, a) for a basket scanned in reverse order, so one pair is counted under two keys; > instead of >=; sorting by count only, so the output order depends on dictionary order; checking max_items against len(basket) instead of distinct items; generating every pair and then discarding bulk baskets; looping over all catalogue pairs.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Lift = P(a and b) / (P(a) · P(b)), or confidence = P(b | a). Both correct for popularity, but they are noisy for rare items, so keep a minimum support or use a shrunk estimate. (2) Map each basket to its pairs and reduce by pair key. The shuffle carries Σ b² records, so combine locally before shuffling, and drop bulk baskets first. Very popular items make some pair keys hot, so a two-stage aggregation helps. (3) Triples grow as Σ b³. Apriori pruning applies: a triple can only be frequent if all three of its pairs are, so generate candidate triples from frequent pairs inside each basket. (4) Compare with the same week last year and with nearby regions, join promotion and planogram calendars, and check basket counts and data completeness for that region before believing it.

def area_sales(grid, queries):
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    P = [[0] * (C + 1)]                    # P[i][j] = total of rows < i and columns < j
    for row in grid:
        above = P[-1]
        cur = [0] * (C + 1)
        run = 0
        for j, v in enumerate(row):
            run += v
            cur[j + 1] = above[j + 1] + run
        P.append(cur)
    out = []
    for r1, c1, r2, c2 in queries:
        if r1 > r2:
            r1, r2 = r2, r1
        if c1 > c2:
            c1, c2 = c2, c1
        r1, c1 = max(r1, 0), max(c1, 0)
        r2, c2 = min(r2, R - 1), min(c2, C - 1)
        if r1 > r2 or c1 > c2:
            out.append(0)                  # no cell of the rectangle is on the floor
            continue
        out.append(P[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - P[r1][c2 + 1] - P[r2 + 1][c1] + P[r1][c1])
    return out

Explanation. A prefix-sum table with one extra row and column of zeros removes every boundary case: P[i][j] is the total of all cells in rows below i and columns below j. A row's running sum plus the row above builds it in one pass. A rectangle is then the large prefix, minus the prefix above it, minus the prefix to its left, plus the corner removed twice. Before the lookup, the corners are put in order, because staff draw from either corner, and clipped to the floor. A rectangle that has no cell on the floor after clipping returns 0 rather than a meaningless lookup.

Complexity. O(R·C) to build and O(1) per rectangle, so O(R·C + q) time and O(R·C) memory. The timing test (600 × 800 cells, 80 000 rectangles, most covering about two thirds of the rows) runs in about 0.15 s in CPython. The "middle" approach a strong candidate may write first is a prefix sum per row (or itertools.accumulate per row) with a loop over the rectangle's rows. That is O(q·rows), about 32 million Python-level steps, and it takes about 13 s, over the 8 s limit and nearly 90 times slower. Summing row slices with sum(grid[r][c1:c2 + 1]) runs each slice at C speed, but it is still one slice per row of every rectangle, about 190 s. NumPy slicing of a 2D array is O(area) per rectangle too. Only the 2D prefix table, in NumPy or not, makes each rectangle O(1).

Dialect notes. In SQL, a summed-area table can be built with window functions (SUM(v) OVER (PARTITION BY col ORDER BY row) and then over columns), and the four-corner lookup is four joins. A plain SUM(...) WHERE row BETWEEN ... AND col BETWEEN ... per rectangle is the per-rectangle scan. In Java or C++, use long for the table: 480 000 cells of up to 10 000 each fit easily, but larger grids or cents can overflow 32 bits. In NumPy, arr.cumsum(0).cumsum(1) padded with zeros builds the same table. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A single cell; the whole floor, including the last row and column; one full row and one full column; no queries; a one-cell floor; the same rectangle twice; at Hard, corners given in any order and a negative cell; at Very Hard, rectangles that run off the floor (clipped), rectangles entirely off it (0), and a rectangle larger than the floor on every side.

Common mistakes. A table without the extra row and column, with r1 - 1 read as index -1 (Python silently wraps to the last row); off-by-one on the inclusive corners; assuming r1 <= r2; clipping only one side; returning a lookup for an empty clipped rectangle (it can be non-zero garbage); summing each rectangle and calling it fast because slices run in C.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A 2D Fenwick tree gives O(log R · log C) for both updates and queries. Alternatively, keep the prefix table and a small list of pending updates added to each query, rebuilding the table every so often. (2) Slide a 3 × 4 window using the prefix table: every position is O(1), so O(R·C) in total. (3) Store a prefix table per store and week only if queries are frequent. Otherwise store the cell grid in a columnar format by store and week, and build tables on demand and cache them. Different floor sizes are just different shapes. (4) Normalise by area, linear feet of shelf or fixture type, or compare each cell with the same fixture type across stores, and say which comparison is fair.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta


def _units_on_order(orders, case_pack):
    return sum(o["cases"] * case_pack for o in orders if o["status"] == "open")   # only orders still to come


def replenishment_orders(positions, forecast, stores, start, end):
    need = {}                                   # (store, item) -> forecast units
    for f in forecast:
        local = datetime.fromisoformat(f["utc"]) + timedelta(hours=stores[f["store"]])
        day = local.date().isoformat()          # the store-local date of the hour
        if start <= day <= end:
            key = (f["store"], f["item"])
            need[key] = need.get(key, 0) + f["units"]
    orders = {}
    for p in positions:
        key = (p["store"], p["item"])
        available = max(p["on_hand"], 0) + p["backroom"]          # the field is "backroom"; negative on-hand is 0
        available += _units_on_order(p["open_orders"], p["case_pack"])
        short = need.get(key, 0) + p["safety"] - available
        if short > 0:
            orders[p["store"] + "/" + p["item"]] = -(-short // p["case_pack"])   # whole cases, rounded up
    return orders

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Rounded down to whole cases. short // case_pack orders the cases that fit inside the shortfall, not the cases that cover it. Symptom: orders arrive one case short, and shelves run out a day early. Fix: round up, -(-short // case_pack) (or (short + case_pack - 1) // case_pack).
  2. Backroom read from a renamed field. p.get("back_room", 0) never finds the backroom key, so backroom stock is always 0, and .get with a default hides the error. Symptom: stores with full backrooms keep receiving more. Fix: read p["backroom"], and prefer indexing to .get with a default for required fields.
  3. Negative on-hand not treated as 0. on_hand + backroom lets a count of −6 cancel six units of backroom or open orders. Symptom: a store whose count went negative after a late receipt over-ordered. Fix: max(on_hand, 0) for the floor count alone.
  4. Received orders counted as still on order. The filter status != "cancelled" keeps "received" orders, which are already in the counts. Symptom: delivered items treated as still on the way, so stores under-order. Fix: count only status == "open".
  5. Forecast bucketed by UTC date. f["utc"][:10] is the UTC date. For a store at UTC−7, the hours from 17:00 local time onwards fall on the next UTC date, so the window takes the previous evening's hours and loses the last evening's. Symptom: stores in the west order for the wrong days. Fix: add the store's offset before taking the date.

Each bug has its own check, built so the other bugs do not change its result: a shortfall of 14 with a case pack of 6 (bug 1); backroom stock with a shortfall that is a whole number of cases (bug 2); a negative on-hand (bug 3); a received and an open order (bug 4); forecast hours either side of local midnight (bug 5). The cancelled-order check passes on the original code; it is there to catch an over-correction such as counting every status except "received". The "exact cover orders nothing" and "no forecast" checks also catch bugs 2 and 1 in a second setting.

Explanation. Replenishment is a position calculation: need (forecast plus safety) against what is or will be in the store (floor, backroom, open orders), turned into whole cases. Each input has a definition that a small code change can break silently: the field name, the meaning of a negative count, which order statuses add future stock, and which local day an hour belongs to.

Complexity. O(F + P) for F forecast rows and P positions, with O(store-items) memory. The timing test (40 000 positions and 200 000 forecast hours) runs in about 0.5 s in CPython. datetime.fromisoformat is the main cost.

Dialect notes. In SQL the forecast step is GROUP BY store, item over (utc_ts + offset_hours * INTERVAL '1 hour')::date BETWEEN :start AND :end, or AT TIME ZONE with a zone name where daylight saving matters. Rounding up is CEIL(short::numeric / case_pack), or the integer form (short + case_pack - 1) / case_pack. Integer division in SQL truncates toward zero, which is the same bug as bug 1. A COALESCE(back_room, 0) on a renamed column is bug 2 in another form. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Rounding a part case up; backroom stock; a negative on-hand; received, open and cancelled orders; forecast hours either side of local midnight at both ends of the window; two stores in different time zones at the same UTC hour; stock that exactly covers need plus safety; a position with no forecast that orders up to safety stock; forecast rows for an item the store does not stock.

Common mistakes. Fixing rounding with round() (rounds a shortfall of 1.4 cases down); clamping on_hand + backroom at 0 instead of on_hand alone; using != "received", which counts cancelled orders; subtracting the offset instead of adding it; keeping .get("back_room", 0) and adding .get("backroom", 0) beside it; rewriting the function instead of making minimal fixes. (math.ceil(short / case_pack) is acceptable at these sizes; it goes through a float, which is worth one question.)

Use the history of forecasts against sales, not just sales. (2) Store the pack size on each open order, so old orders convert with the pack they were placed in. Version the item's pack with effective dates. (3) Repeated negatives for the same items point to receiving or scanning process problems. Rank store-items by how often and how far they go negative, and schedule cycle counts there. (4) Schedule each store's run after its local close, in time-zone waves. Treat late forecasts or receipts as inputs to the next run, and alert when a run uses stale inputs.

Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Events, keyed and deduplicated. order_placed and line_edited (order id, line id, item, quantity, estimated weight, unit price per kg or per pack, estimate in cents, price version). line_picked (line id, pick id, measured grams or label price and grams, scale or label source, device id, store). line_substituted (original line id, substitute line id, rule used). line_short (quantity not found). handed_over (order id, final total, captured amount). line_returned (line id, returned grams or quantity, refund in cents). Every event carries an event id generated on the device. The pipeline deduplicates on it, so a resend after reconnecting is a no-op.
  • Line model. order_line keeps the estimate and never changes after the order is placed (edits create a new version). fulfilment_line holds what was picked: one or more picks per ordered line, a substitute linked to the original, and the short quantity. charge_line holds the final price inputs (grams, price per kg, price version, rule version) and the rounded amount, computed once with this exercise's rule (half up to the cent). Returns link to the charge line.
  • Final charge. final per line = round_half_up(grams × price_per_kg / 1000) in integer arithmetic (for example (grams * price_cents_per_kg + 500) // 1000). The price version is the one in force at the pick, or the lower of the order-time and pick-time prices, stated as this exercise's rule and recorded on the line. The order total is the sum of line totals, so it reconciles exactly.
  • Over-buffer handling. If the final total exceeds the authorised amount, the options are a re-authorisation for the difference, capping the charge at the authorised amount and absorbing the difference, or asking the customer at handover. Record which happened (capture_mode). The analytics track the rate and the amount absorbed.
  • Receipts. The customer receipt is rendered from the charge lines and their recorded inputs, so it can be rebuilt exactly months later. Nothing is recomputed from the current price file.
  • Analytics (aggregate). Estimate accuracy per item, store and week (final over estimated, distribution of the ratio); the share of orders above the buffer, and the amount; estimated, authorised and captured revenue per day; substitution and short rates for weighed lines. No customer-level reporting.

Competing designs to accept. One wide line table with an estimate snapshot and actual columns (fine if the estimate is never overwritten and picks are not limited to one per line); event-sourced line state with a materialised current view; streaming computation of final charges at handover with a nightly batch for analytics. Any is acceptable if the inputs to each charge are stored and the rounding rule is stated.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Overwriting the estimate with the actual; floats for weights or prices; recomputing old receipts from today's prices; a substitution that loses the link to the original line; double-counted picks after a device resend; per-unit rounding summed into a line total that does not match the receipt.

  • Deli prices ten times too high for three hours: find the affected lines by price version and store (the price version on each charge line makes this a query). Refund the difference per line in cents. Correct the price file with a new version, and add a guard that rejects a price change above a set ratio without approval. Report the impact in aggregate.
  • 3% of orders exceed the buffer on a holiday, and captured revenue exceeds authorised: confirm whether re-authorisations or absorbed differences explain it, by capture_mode. A report showing captured above authorised with no re-authorisation recorded is a data bug, so check the join. Use the distribution of final over estimated per item to set the buffer for peak days.
  • Pick events sent twice after reconnecting: deduplication on the device's event id makes the second copy a no-op. Monitor the duplicate rate per device. If two different weights arrive for one pick id, keep both, flag the line, and use the rule (for example, the latest by device sequence) recorded on the charge line.

(1) Query the picks by scale id and date range, estimate the error from the calibration result, refund overcharged lines (and decide on undercharges as a policy), and add calibration status to the scale reference data. (2) Re-authorise, cap and absorb, or confirm with the customer. Choose the buffer from the distribution of final over estimated per item and order mix, weighed against failed re-authorisations. (3) Refund = round_half_up(returned grams × charged price per kg). The charge line gains a return row, and the original stays unchanged. (4) Monitor final over estimated per item and region weekly. A persistent bias goes to merchandising to update the average weight, versioned with an effective date.

WMT-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Transaction identity. (store, register, register_sequence, register_boot_id), created on the register. The boot id (or an epoch counter) separates a sequence that restarts after a reinstall. A resend carries the same identity, and the ingestion layer upserts by it, so a transaction counts once.
  • Store-and-forward. Each register keeps a local journal and forwards it in sequence order when connected. The store's gateway acknowledges by sequence. A per-register high-water mark plus a set of gaps shows exactly what is missing. Ingestion lands raw journal batches immutably, with arrival time, before parsing.
  • Record shape. Header (identity, status complete or voided, register timestamp, store-local business date, cashier lane type), lines (item, quantity, price in cents, department, line void linking to the voided line with a negative quantity), tenders (type, amount), and returns (lines with negative quantity, the original transaction identity when the receipt is known, the return store).
  • Business date. The store-local date of the transaction's completion, by this exercise's rule, with stores' zones from reference data. A transaction that crosses midnight belongs to its completion date. Clock checks compare the register timestamp with arrival time and with neighbouring sequence numbers. A register whose clock disagrees beyond a threshold is flagged, and its transactions are dated by the sequence position between trusted neighbours, or by the arrival date, recorded as a correction.
  • Daily tables, versioned. sales_daily (store, business_date, department, item, units, net_cents, version) is rebuilt per store and date when new transactions arrive for it. Each rebuild is a new version, with a change log (store, date, old_total, new_total, transactions added). Analysts see the latest version, and finance can see what was published when.
  • Reconciliation. Per store, date, register and tender: analytics totals against the till close. States: matched, pending (sequence gaps not yet filled), explained difference (late transactions after close, returns of online orders recorded elsewhere) and unexplained, with the registers and transaction ids listed. A store and day is final only when the gaps are closed and the totals match or the difference is explained.
  • Fast path. Item-level sales stream within minutes for replenishment and price analytics, labelled provisional. The nightly reconciled tables are the record.

Competing designs to accept. Streaming ingestion with a lakehouse table merged by transaction identity and nightly partition rebuilds; a batch-only design with hourly loads (fine if late data and versions are handled); event-sourced daily totals with corrections as delta rows. Any is acceptable if a transaction counts once, late data is explainable, and the reconciliation names the transactions behind a difference.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Deduplicating on the register timestamp instead of a register-generated identity; a sequence restart read as a huge gap or as duplicates; business dates from UTC or from arrival time; line voids dropped or double-negated; returns credited to the original store; silently overwriting published days; reconciliation only at store level, which hides a single register's problem.

Incident guidance.

  • Region offline for {{offline_hours}}, backlog forwarded with resends: deduplication on the transaction identity absorbs the resends. Watch ingestion lag and the duplicate rate. The affected stores stay pending until sequence gaps close, then their days are rebuilt as new versions. Reconciliation runs again after the till close, which may come before the backlog lands.
  • Register clock in the wrong time zone after a repair: clock checks flag it, because register time disagrees with arrival time and with neighbouring registers. Re-date its transactions with the documented rule, rebuild the two affected days for that store, record the correction, and add a clock check to the repair checklist.
  • 30 stores below the till close after a software update changed line voids: reconciliation shows unexplained differences concentrated on registers running the new version. Find the new void representation in the raw journals (they are kept), fix the parser, reprocess the affected days from raw data, and add a contract test on void lines for future updates.

Follow-up guidance. (1) During the outage, the fast path shows a drop for those stores and labels it. After reconnection, the backlog lands, days are rebuilt as new versions, and the change log shows the additions. After the till close, reconciliation matches or names the gaps. (2) Detect it with register time against arrival time and with neighbouring registers. Date the transactions by sequence position or arrival, and record the correction. (3) Compare per register and tender, list missing sequence numbers and transactions after close, check returns and voids. Finance signs off on explained differences. (4) A streaming path labelled provisional, and the reconciled nightly path as the record, with the difference between them monitored.

Rubric anchors. 2: sales loaded by timestamp and appended; no transaction identity; reconciliation as a single number. 3: register-generated identity with deduplication, sequence-gap completeness, explicit voids and returns, store-local business dates, versioned rebuilds of late days, per-register reconciliation. 4: also clock-drift detection and correction, a provisional fast path separated from the reconciled record, raw journals kept for reprocessing, and a credible response to each incident.

Strong signals. Uses register sequence numbers to prove completeness; asks how a sequence restart is told apart from a gap; treats the till close as an input to reconcile against, not something to overwrite. Red flags. "Use the register timestamp as the key"; adjusting analytics totals to match the tills without explaining the difference.

WMT-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Items and offers. items (item_id, product_group_id, upc, description, department, category, is_weighted); variants are items sharing a product_group_id. offers (offer_id, item_id, channel store|online|marketplace, seller_id, store_id NULL): one row per store item, one for the retailer's online offer, and one per marketplace seller offer (the retailer itself is not a marketplace seller here; its online offer is channel online).
  • Zones. price_zones (zone_id, name) and zone_membership (store_id, zone_id, valid_from_date, valid_to_date), effective-dated by store-local date. Never a zone_id column on the store row alone.
  • Price records (decisions). price_records (price_record_id, item_id, scope_type zone|store|online|seller_offer, scope_id, price_type regular|rollback|clearance|online_only, amount_cents, reference_cents NULL, valid_from, valid_to NULL, recorded_at, superseded_at NULL, supersedes_id NULL, source, reason). valid_from/valid_to is when the price is in force (store prices as a local date; online as an instant); recorded_at/superseded_at is when the system believed the record. A correction inserts a new record that supersedes_id the old one and sets the old one's superseded_at (the only update ever made, and an append-only design can derive it instead).
  • Resolution (this exercise's precedence). For (offer, date): take records in force on that date and not superseded as of the "believed at" time; rank clearance > rollback > regular; within a type, a store-scope record beats the zone record; the store's zone is the one in zone_membership on that date. The "was" price for a rollback is the regular price that would have applied on that date without it. An overlap of two records of the same type and scope is a data-quality violation: reject at write time, or resolve by latest recorded_at and flag it.
  • Derived price of record. price_of_record (offer_id, valid_from, valid_to, amount_cents, price_type, was_cents, winning_record_id) as intervals (not one row per day), maintained incrementally: a new or corrected record recomputes only the affected offers and dates. Store-level intervals can be derived per zone and expanded only for stores with exceptions, which keeps the table near zones × items rather than stores × items.
  • Questions answered. "Price on D" = the interval containing D; "what did we believe on D" = re-run resolution with records where recorded_at <= D_end AND (superseded_at IS NULL OR superseded_at > D_end), or keep the derived table bitemporal too.
  • Marketplace. Seller prices are price_records with scope seller_offer, written only from seller feeds; they never participate in the retailer's precedence. What a customer saw is answered from the page/offer log (see WMT-L3-04) plus these records.

Competing designs to accept. A fully bitemporal table with both axes as ranges (tstzrange plus an exclusion constraint) instead of supersedes links. An event-sourced price log with the resolved table as a projection. Per-day snapshots for the last N days plus intervals for older history, if the candidate costs it. Resolution done on read with a cache, if they explain the latency and reproduce history correctly.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. One mutable price column; zone stored on the store row; time zones ignored for store-local effective dates; one row per store × item × day at {{stores}} stores (billions of rows a day); no second time axis, so late and corrected records are indistinguishable; marketplace prices mixed with retailer precedence; overlaps of clearance and rollback not detected; recomputing the whole history after each of {{weekly_changes}} changes.

Incident guidance.

  • Re-zoning changed last quarter's report: zone was overwritten on the store row. Restore history by building zone_membership from change logs or snapshots, rerun the report from effective-dated membership, and add a check that historical reports are stable when only future membership changes.
  • Rollback ends loaded in UTC: store prices take effect at the store-local day boundary. Correct with superseding records (not edits) carrying the local date, re-derive the affected intervals, and reconcile register charged prices for the hours affected; add validation that store-scope effective times are local dates.
  • Clearance and rollback both active: precedence must reject or resolve the conflict at write time. Supersede the rollback in the 400 stores, recompute the price of record, fix the "was" price derivation (it must be the regular price, and a rollback on a clearance item is not allowed), and alert on overlaps of incompatible types.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Filter in force on D, not superseded; ORDER BY type rank, scope rank, recorded_at DESC; take first. (2) Old record superseded, new record with the shorter end; "believed on Thursday" returns the shortened one only if it was recorded before Thursday's end; otherwise the original. (3) Only zone_membership rows change; last month's history is unchanged because resolution uses membership on the date. (4) Intervals per zone and item plus store exceptions; estimate: items × zones × changes per year, versus stores × items × days. (5) The seller's offer record plus a log of the offer and price shown at order time; without a logged snapshot, a later reconstruction may not match what was on screen.

Rubric anchors. 2: a price column per item (maybe per store) updated in place; no history or only SCD2 with one time axis; zone on the store row. 3: typed effective-dated records, zone membership over time, stated precedence, resolved intervals, store-local dates. 4: also bitemporal corrections, "was" price, incremental recompute sized with numbers, marketplace prices kept apart, and incident fixes by supersession.

Strong signals. Separates decisions from resolved prices; asks how corrections are dated; sizes the derived table. Red flags. Overwrites prices; computes the price on a date from today's zone; stores money as floating point.

WMT-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Orders. orders (order_id, store_id, slot_start, slot_end, channel pickup|delivery, placed_at); order_lines (order_line_id, order_id, item_id, requested_qty, uom each|kg, est_price_cents, sub_preference any|named|none, named_sub_item_id NULL).
  • Picking. pick_walks (walk_id, store_id, started_at, ended_at, temp_zone) with no person identifier in analytics (the operational system may hold a device id; it is not replicated). pick_events (pick_event_id, walk_id, order_line_id, tote_id, kind picked|short|substituted, item_id, qty, measured_weight NULL, recorded_at). A substitution is a pick event with kind = substituted and its own item_id, plus substitutions (substitution_id, order_line_id, ordered_item_id, sub_item_id, qty, offered_price_cents, charged_cap_cents).
  • Totes and staging. totes (tote_id, order_id, temp_zone) (one order per tote); tote_moves (tote_id, location_id, moved_at) with staging_locations (location_id, store_id, kind shelf|cooler|freezer|bay_cooler). Time in staging = intervals between consecutive moves until handoff, computed with LEAD over moves per tote.
  • Handoff. handoffs (handoff_id, order_id, handed_at, kind customer|driver, no_show bool); substitution_decisions (substitution_id, decision accepted|rejected, decided_at).
  • Line outcome (analytics). fct_line_outcome (order_line_id, store_id, local_date, department, requested_qty, picked_as_ordered_qty, substituted_qty, sub_accepted_qty, sub_rejected_qty, short_qty, est_amount_cents, charged_cents) with the invariant requested = as_ordered + substituted + short (for weighted items, in the ordered unit with a stated tolerance). Built incrementally from events by order (an accumulating snapshot that closes at handoff).
  • Metrics (per store, department, day; aggregates only). Fill rate = Σ as-ordered units ÷ Σ requested; substitution rate = Σ substituted ÷ Σ requested; acceptance rate = Σ accepted ÷ Σ substitutes presented at handoff (no-shows excluded and reported apart); short with no substitute offered = Σ short where preference allowed one; staging breach count per temp zone = totes with chilled/frozen staging time over {{staging_limit_minutes}} minutes.

Competing designs to accept. Line outcome as an event-sourced fold, recomputed per order on each event. A single line_events table with a typed event column instead of separate pick/substitution tables, if quantities still reconcile. Weighted items modelled with a separate estimated and actual quantity on the line outcome.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A single status on the line; substitutes overwriting the ordered item; associate ids leaking into the warehouse or being used for per-person metrics; staging time from one overwritten staged_at; mixed time zones between devices; nightly full rebuilds at {{orders_per_day}} orders × {{lines_per_order}} lines; acceptance rates with an unclear denominator.

Incident guidance.

  • Rejected recorded as accepted: identify the release window and stores, rebuild decisions from the handoff device's raw events if kept (or mark the window as unknown), issue refunds through the payment system for rejected-and-charged substitutes, write correction rows (never edit the outcome silently), recompute the affected days and annotate the metric. Guardrail: a contract test that the decision field round-trips; alert on sudden acceptance-rate jumps per store.
  • Staging times inflated: one move type logged in local time. Normalise all event times to UTC with the store's zone at ingestion, recompute intervals for the affected period, and add a validation that moves for a tote are monotonic in time.
  • Nightly rebuild too slow: switch to incremental builds keyed by orders touched since the last watermark (orders close at handoff, so late events are bounded), partition by store-local date, and keep a weekly full reconciliation.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Σ outcome qty per line = requested; violations go to a quarantine table and an alert, never silently dropped. (2) Store both 2 kg requested and 2.3 kg picked; the charge is per this exercise's rule (the actual weight at the per-kg price, within a tolerance, or capped — candidate states it); fill rate counts the line as filled within tolerance. (3) Acceptance = accepted ÷ presented; no-shows are not decisions. (4) Two tote_moves rows and the handoff; breach when staged time exceeds the limit; report per store, day and temperature zone. (5) Facts: pick events (event grain), tote moves, handoffs; the accumulating line outcome snapshot.

Rubric anchors. 2: one status per line, substitutes overwrite the item, staging as a single timestamp, per-picker metrics. 3: outcome rows that reconcile, substitution as its own record, totes and moves, precise metrics per store and day. 4: also weighted items, privacy by grain (no associate ids in analytics), incremental builds and correct incident repairs.

Strong signals. Writes the reconciliation invariant unprompted; defines denominators. Red flags. Ranking stores' or associates' "productivity" from pick times; editing outcomes without a correction trail.

WMT-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Reference data. items, case_packs (item_id, units_per_case, valid_from, valid_to), dcs, stores, suppliers (supplier_id) as ids only.
  • Inbound. purchase_orders (po_id, dc_id, supplier_id, expected_at), po_lines (po_id, item_id, cases_ordered, crossdock bool). case_events (event_id, case_label, item_id, dc_id, kind received|put_away|allocated|unallocated|picked|loaded|unloaded|departed|store_received|store_short|written_off, store_id NULL, trailer_trip_id NULL, location_id NULL, event_at, recorded_at, device_id). received captures units_per_case as of that moment (copied from case_packs) so later conversions never use today's pack.
  • Allocations. Cross-dock allocations are created before arrival from po_lines and store orders; storage allocations after putaway. Both are allocated events on cases (or allocation_lines (allocation_id, dc_id, item_id, store_id, cases, created_at, superseded_by) with cases bound at pick time).
  • Outbound. trailer_trips (trip_id, dc_id, departed_at), trip_stops (trip_id, stop_seq, store_id); loaded and departed events per case.
  • State on D. case_state_asof(D) = latest event per case with event_at <= D_end (dedup by event_id, and by (case_label, kind, event_at) for resent scans); states: in_storage, allocated_not_shipped, in_transit(store), received_at_store, written_off. Units = Σ units_per_case captured at receipt.
  • Conservation per DC and item. received = in storage + allocated not shipped + shipped + written off, checked daily; shipped = in transit + received at stores + store shortages under investigation.
  • Physical design. Events partitioned by event date and DC; a daily snapshot of open cases (cases not yet received at a store or written off) so "as of D" reads the snapshot for D−1 plus one day of events; late events trigger a re-snapshot of the affected days.

Competing designs to accept. Quantity-based flows (lots of N cases) instead of per-case identity, if conversions and partial picks are handled. A pallet-level model with cases as children. Event sourcing with a state table updated in the same transaction as each event, as long as history by date is reproducible.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A mutable current location as the only state; summing events instead of taking the latest per case; converting with today's case pack; duplicate scans; cross-dock cases that fall out of every state when allocations are cancelled; full scans of all events for every as-of query at {{cases_per_day}} cases a day; time zones of DCs and stores mixed.

Incident guidance.

  • Resent "loaded" scans: counting loads, not states. Deduplicate by event id (or label, kind and event time), compute state as the latest event per case, rerun the affected day's snapshot, and add a monitor comparing in-transit units with loaded-not-received cases.
  • Case pack conversion: capture units per case on the receipt event; restate the affected shipments using the captured pack; add a check that conversions use the pack valid at receipt.
  • Orphan cases after cancelled allocations: an unallocated event must return the case to a state (awaiting putaway). Backfill the state for the orphaned cases, make "no state" impossible by a constraint or a daily conservation check, and report the cross-dock share from cases that actually flowed through, not from the plan, with {{crossdock_share}} as the plan.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Latest event per case at D_end with DISTINCT ON (case_label) … ORDER BY case_label, event_at DESC, recorded_at DESC filtered to departed; group by store and item, sum units. (2) Old cases convert at 12, new at 8; the store's receipt uses the pack captured on the case. (3) Two store_short events and one store_received at the wrong store plus a transfer or return event; conservation holds per DC because each case is in exactly one state. (4) Snapshot of open cases daily versus compute on demand; cost in rows and recompute after late events. (5) Final after the lateness bound (two days here); show provisional numbers with a watermark.

Rubric anchors. 2: a current-location table, cases and units mixed, no as-of capability. 3: case events with event and recorded times, cross-dock and storage paths, state as latest event, case pack captured, conservation stated. 4: also deduplication, orphan prevention, snapshot strategy sized against volume, lateness and provisional numbers, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Picks the case label as identity; writes the conservation equation. Red flags. Converting with the current case pack; updating rows in place; counting scans as movements.

WMT-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Catalogue and sellers. items (item_id, product_group_id), sellers (seller_id, is_retailer), seller_standing (seller_id, as_of_date, on_time_rate, valid_tracking_rate, meets_minimums, inputs_complete) recomputed daily (this exercise's rule).
  • Offers. offers (offer_id, item_id, seller_id, condition); offer_versions (offer_id, version, price_cents, shipping_cents, qty_available, delivery_promise_days, event_at, recorded_at, source) append-only; the current version per offer is the one with the latest event_at (with recorded_at as a tie-break), and an out-of-order update older than the current one is stored but does not change the present.
  • Decisions. featured_decisions (decision_id, item_id, decided_at, trigger offer_update|standing_change|stock_out|rule_change, rule_version, chosen_offer_id NULL, chosen_version NULL); decision_inputs (decision_id, offer_id, version, eligible, ineligible_reason, total_price_cents, score NULL, score_version NULL, rank) so the choice under {{featured_rule}} is reproducible. featured_intervals (item_id, offer_id NULL, valid_from, valid_to, decision_id) non-overlapping per item (an exclusion constraint on a range, or closing each interval at the next interval's start in the same time axis). offer_id NULL means "no eligible offer".
  • Time axes. Decisions are recomputed on event time for history ("who should have been featured") and the live system logs what was served (page_views are not stored per customer; order lines store it).
  • Orders. order_lines (order_line_id, item_id, offer_id, offer_version, featured_decision_id, price_cents): what the customer bought, and what was featured at that moment.
  • Queries. Share of featured time per seller, item and week: intersect each interval with the week ([max(from, week_start), min(to, week_end))), sum durations, divide by the week's length. Share of orders: count order lines by featured_decision_id's chosen seller. "Why not S at T": the decision active at T and its decision_inputs row for S (ineligible reason or rank and the featured total price), filtered to S's own rows plus the fields the rule exposes.
  • Scale. At {{offer_updates}} updates a day, offer versions are partitioned by day and clustered by item; decisions are recomputed only for items whose offers or sellers changed; a standing change fans out through an index of (seller → items with offers).

Competing designs to accept. Computing the featured offer on read with a cache, plus a decision log written on change (history must still exist). Storing only decisions with inputs and deriving intervals as a view. A stream processor keyed by item maintaining the current choice, with the log as its output.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Offers overwritten; a featured flag on the offer row (two flags at once, no history); intervals closed on recorded time and opened on event time (overlaps); no "none eligible" state; standing computed from incomplete inputs; sellers seeing competitors' details; re-evaluating all {{items}} items when standing changes.

Incident guidance.

  • Backlogged updates: decisions and intervals built on recorded time penalised sellers for delay in ingestion. Recompute history on event time from stored versions; keep "what was served" separately from the decision log; communicate to affected sellers with the corrected share of featured time.
  • Standing input missing: an incomplete input should keep the previous standing (or mark it unknown and not change eligibility), never mark everyone ineligible. Re-run standing with the input, recompute decisions for affected items, and add inputs_complete as a gate.
  • Shares adding to 107%: intervals on mixed time axes overlap. Rebuild intervals on one axis, add a non-overlap constraint per item, and assert shares sum to at most 100% per item and week.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Interval-week intersection, including those still open (valid_to NULL → now). (2) Event-time history says the seller was featured from 12:00 if their new price wins; what the customer saw (served log) shows the old choice until 12:10; both are true for their own questions. (3) Fan out from the three sellers to items with their offers; recompute those decisions only. (4) The decision and its inputs for S, the featured offer's exposed fields only. (5) Partitioned versions, current-state table for the page, intervals table for history.

Rubric anchors. 2: offers overwritten, a flag for the featured offer, no history or reasons. 3: offer versions, eligibility with reasons, featured intervals with decisions, order lines linked to versions. 4: also two time axes handled deliberately, reproducible selections with rule and score versions, seller-scoped evidence, incremental recompute with fan-out, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Distinguishes "who should have been featured" from "what was served"; models "none eligible". Red flags. Showing sellers competitors' data; overlapping intervals; recomputing the whole catalogue on every change.

WMT-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH windows AS (
  SELECT rollback_id, item_id, region, 'rollback' AS phase, start_date AS first_day, end_date AS last_day
  FROM rollbacks
  UNION ALL
  SELECT rollback_id, item_id, region, 'baseline', start_date - 28, start_date - 1
  FROM rollbacks
), store_days AS (
  SELECT w.rollback_id, w.item_id, w.phase, s.store_id, s.region, s.opened_on, w.first_day + k AS day
  FROM windows w
  JOIN stores s ON s.region = w.region
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(0, w.last_day - w.first_day) AS k
), counted AS (
  SELECT sd.rollback_id, sd.item_id, sd.phase, sd.store_id, sd.day
  FROM store_days sd
  WHERE sd.day >= sd.opened_on
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM out_of_stock_days o
                    WHERE o.store_id = sd.store_id AND o.item_id = sd.item_id AND o.oos_date = sd.day)
    AND NOT (sd.phase = 'baseline' AND EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM rollbacks r2
          WHERE r2.item_id = sd.item_id AND r2.region = sd.region AND r2.rollback_id <> sd.rollback_id
            AND sd.day BETWEEN r2.start_date AND r2.end_date))
), rates AS (
  SELECT c.rollback_id, c.phase, COUNT(*) AS store_days, SUM(COALESCE(f.units, 0)) AS units
  FROM counted c
  LEFT JOIN store_item_sales f
    ON f.store_id = c.store_id AND f.item_id = c.item_id AND f.sale_date = c.day
  GROUP BY c.rollback_id, c.phase
)
SELECT r.rollback_id,
       r.item_id,
       ro.store_days AS rollback_store_days,
       ROUND(ro.units::numeric / ro.store_days, 2) AS rollback_units_per_store_day,
       COALESCE(b.store_days, 0) AS baseline_store_days,
       ROUND(b.units::numeric / b.store_days, 2) AS baseline_units_per_store_day,
       CASE WHEN b.units > 0
            THEN ROUND(100.0 * ro.units * b.store_days / (ro.store_days * b.units) - 100, 1)
       END AS lift_pct
FROM rollbacks r
JOIN rates ro ON ro.rollback_id = r.rollback_id AND ro.phase = 'rollback'
LEFT JOIN rates b ON b.rollback_id = r.rollback_id AND b.phase = 'baseline'
ORDER BY r.rollback_id;

Explanation. The denominator is store-days, and a store-day exists whether or not anything sold, so it has to come from a calendar: each rollback's two windows expanded to dates and crossed with the stores in its region. Store-days before a store opened, store-days when the item was out of stock and (at the hardest level) baseline days inside another rollback of the same item in the same region are removed as whole store-days, units included; only then are sales LEFT JOINed and summed with zeros filled in. The two windows are aggregated separately and placed side by side. The lift is written as one division of exact integers, 100 × rollback units × baseline days ÷ (rollback days × baseline units) − 100, so it is exact before the single rounding; a zero baseline gives NULL rather than an error.

Complexity. The calendar has Σ over rollbacks of (window days × stores in region) rows: about 36 × stores per rollback. The anti-joins and the sales join are hash or index lookups on (store_id, item_id, date). In production, a daily store-item fact with an in-stock flag and explicit zero rows (or a store-item-day calendar table) replaces the generated series, and readouts are incremental per rollback.

Dialect notes. generate_series with CROSS JOIN LATERAL is PostgreSQL; BigQuery uses UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(first_day, last_day)), Snowflake a row generator or a calendar table (TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n)) with DATEADD), Spark SQL explode(sequence(first_day, last_day)), MySQL 8 a recursive CTE or a calendar table. date - integer is PostgreSQL; others use DATE_SUB/DATEADD. Division: units / store_days truncates to an integer in PostgreSQL, while Snowflake and MySQL return a decimal and BigQuery and Spark SQL a floating-point value; an explicit cast to NUMERIC/DECIMAL keeps the result portable. ROUND on numeric rounds halves away from zero in PostgreSQL; BigQuery ROUND on FLOAT64 also rounds half away from zero but floating point may land just below a half, so use NUMERIC. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. Sales the day before the baseline (start − 29) and the day after the rollback (end + 1), which must not count; the first baseline day and the last rollback day, which must; out-of-stock store-days with units sold before the stock-out, in both windows. Hard adds a second region (stores outside a rollback's region sell the item too), sales rows only on days with sales, and a seasonal item whose baseline sold nothing (lift NULL, baseline rate 0.00). Very Hard adds a store that opened inside a baseline window (no rows before opening, which a calendar built from all stores would count as zeros), an earlier rollback of the same item in the same region inside a later rollback's baseline, and a rollback of the same item in the other region during that baseline, which must not be excluded.

Common mistakes. Averaging only the sales rows present (zero days lost); starting from store_item_sales with an inner join; dropping out-of-stock store-days from the count but keeping their units; including the start date in the baseline (BETWEEN start_date - 28 AND start_date); treating end_date as exclusive; counting stores from other regions; integer division; rounding the rates before computing lift; (Very Hard) counting pre-opening days, keeping overlapping rollback days in the baseline, or excluding another region's rollback days. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Holdout stores chosen before the start (random within region or matched on prior sales), recorded with the rollback; difference-in-differences between rollback and holdout stores over the same window. (2) Add a similar-items list (same category or a substitution group) and compute the same rates for those items in the same stores and windows; net lift = item lift minus loss on substitutes. (3) In-stock hours as a fractional denominator (store-day weighted by hours on shelf); usually worth it only for fast sellers. (4) A store-item-day fact with in-stock flag and zero rows, partitioned by date; per-rollback aggregates recomputed only when late sales, out-of-stock corrections or rollback edits touch their windows.

Rubric anchors. 2: rates over sales rows only, or out-of-stock handled on one side only. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the holdout design, cannibalisation, and incremental materialisation with explicit zero rows.

Strong signals. Asks immediately whether zero-sale days have rows; treats the denominator as a calendar. Red flags. AVG(units) over the sales table; NOT IN against a nullable column without thought; a lift computed from rounded rates.
